summary: Mauritania scrapped its visa on arrival in January 2025 — nearly all visitors now pre-apply online through the official ANRPTS eVisa portal and pay EUR 55 in cash when they land (EUR 40 for nationals of Arab and African countries), while citizens of eleven neighboring West African and Maghreb states enter visa-free under bilateral agreements.

travelInsurance.text: No official source makes insurance a condition of entry. The UK government advises insurance for local treatment and medical evacuation: medical facilities are extremely limited, particularly outside Nouakchott and Nouadhibou, and clinics charge for care, sometimes in euros or US dollars.

currencyLimits.text: It is illegal to take Mauritanian ouguiyas out of the country, and the authorities may confiscate them. No official source we could read publishes a threshold for declaring foreign currency. US dollars and euros can be exchanged at banks, some hotels and official bureaux de change.

source.name: UK Foreign, Commonwealth & Development Office — Mauritania travel advice (safety and security)

notes: Alcohol may not be brought into Mauritania. It is a dry country and importing it is prohibited.
Drones and professional camera equipment can attract questions at the border. Carry paperwork for anything valuable.

payments.text: Cards work only at a handful of Nouakchott hotels and supermarkets. This is a cash economy. Change euros or dollars at banks or licensed bureaux; locals often still quote prices in pre-2018 "old" ouguiya (ten times the current unit), so confirm which is meant.

safety.text: The west-coast corridor (Nouakchott, Nouadhibou, Banc d'Arguin) and the western Adrar around Atar, Chinguetti and Ouadane see travelers routinely. The UK Foreign Office advises against all travel to the east and to within 25 km of the Mali border because of terrorism risk, and against all but essential travel to much of the rest of the interior, including the southern provinces. Petty crime is moderate; the bigger constraints are distance, heat and thin infrastructure.

source.name: UK Foreign, Commonwealth & Development Office — Mauritania travel advice

bestTimeToVisit.text: November to March is the cool season — the only comfortable window for the Sahara, the Adrar oases and the iron-ore train; from April the interior becomes dangerously hot.

tips.text: Stay out of the areas near the Mali border and the far east. They are under do-not-travel advisories. Stick to the west-coast corridor and the Adrar, ideally with a local operator.
Bring the eVisa fee in exact cash — euros or US dollars. Cards are not accepted at the airport counters and change is rarely given.
Police checkpoints are frequent on every intercity road. Carry a stack of printed passport copies ("fiches") listing your details and route to hand over — it saves long stops.
Mauritania is a dry country — alcohol may not be imported or consumed, including anything bought in duty-free en route.

The Nouadhibou–Zouérat iron-ore train can be ridden by travelers, but conditions in the open ore wagons are harsh. Bring goggles, warm layers for the night and water, or book the single passenger carriage.

faq.question: Do I need a visa for Mauritania?
faq.answer: Most nationalities do. Since January 2025 you must apply online for an eVisa through the official ANRPTS portal before travel, then pay the fee — EUR 55 for 30 days, or EUR 40 for nationals of Arab and African countries — in cash on arrival. Citizens of eleven neighboring West African and Maghreb states (including Algeria, Tunisia, Senegal and Mali) enter visa-free under reciprocal agreements; the Foreign Ministry does not state how long they may stay.

faq.question: Can I still get a Mauritania visa on arrival?
faq.answer: No. The old walk-up visa on arrival was discontinued on January 5, 2025. You must now be pre-approved online via the ANRPTS eVisa portal before boarding; the fee itself is still collected in cash at the border, together with your biometrics.

faq.question: Do I need a yellow fever certificate for Mauritania?
faq.answer: Only if you arrive from a country with risk of yellow fever transmission — common on overland routes from Senegal or Mali. The vaccine is recommended for most travelers regardless, so carry your yellow card.

faq.question: Is Mauritania safe to visit?
faq.answer: The traveled west of the country — Nouakchott, Nouadhibou, the Banc d'Arguin coast and the Adrar — has a growing tourist circuit and is generally calm, but border areas with Mali and the remote east are high-risk and under do-not-travel advisories. Check current advisories and use a local operator for desert itineraries.

faq.question: Can I pay by card in Mauritania?
faq.answer: Rarely — outside a few Nouakchott hotels it is cash only. Bring euros or US dollars to exchange, and note that prices are sometimes quoted in "old" ouguiya worth a tenth of the current MRU unit.
